newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan president vows to hold polls on time.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan president vows to hold polls on time.

text.p: Pakistani President Farooq Leghari said on Monday an interim cabinet that replaced the "incorrigible" government of Benazir Bhutto would fight corruption, pursue economic reform and hold elections on time.
He likened Bhutto, 43, to France's Louis XIV, saying she could not differentiate between state and government.
Leghari, who has kept out of the public eye, partly because of kidney stone trouble, since sacking Bhutto on November 5, said elections would be held as scheduled.
"They will be held on February 3," he said. "I feel it is absolutely vital to hold elections in 90 days."

Leghari, 56, said it was physically impossible to hold a long-overdue national census before the polls, but promised to strengthen the electoral commission and invite international observers to ensure the elections were free and fair.
Leghari named a caretaker cabinet led by Meraj Khalid after dissolving the National Assembly (lower house) and dismissing Bhutto's government on charges of corruption and misrule.
He said he had used presidential powers he had once condemned because he felt that Pakistan was foundering.

"I felt that the state was in danger of collapse," he said. "There was a danger of Pakistan defaulting...Decisions in the (cabinet) were being made not on considerations of national security or interest, but were being taken for other reasons...

"We were in the vortex of crisis for some time," he said. "And I could foresee very clearly the economy collapsing (which) could have led to very grave security concerns and even, God forbid, to the collapse of the state."
Leghari said Bhutto had rejected his advice and warnings that the government should stop what he called its attacks on the judicial system, tackle corruption and change its style.
"Within the prime minister's house there were two fountains of power," he said, referring to Bhutto and her husband, Asif Ali Zardari, who was investment minister in her cabinet.

"Who does not know that federal secretaries of the economic ministries would go to pay homage to the spouse of the prime minister in the prime minister's house? That deals used be struck there and the economic coordination committee of the cabinet and the cabinet were used as rubber-stamping bodies?"
Zardari was detained after Bhutto's dismissal under a maintenance of public order law. The caretaker government has promised to bring undisclosed charges against him and Bhutto.
Leghari, a former close political ally of Bhutto, said that removing her had been "the most painful decision of my life".

He had tried to persuade Bhutto to end a confrontation with the judiciary that began in March when she showed reluctance to implement a Supreme Court ruling that effectively challenged the prime minister's power to appoint higher court judges.

Leghari said that at one meeting Bhutto had argued the Supreme Court chief justice was part of her government. She repeated her view when he asked her if she did not see the distinction between the state and the government.
"I asked her, "Are you Louis XIV?'" he said.
The last straw, Leghari said, came when Bhutto tabled an anti-corruption bill in parliament that he described as a "big joke" and a "further assault on the judiciary".

"It was around that time that I realised that there could be no correction possible," he declared. "It was then that I decided it was impossible for Pakistan to carry on like that without risking economic and state collapse."
